# Reproducible Pipelines with targets {#sec-targets}

Table 2 of a trial manuscript reports the primary outcome by arm.
It was built from an analysis-set file that a cleaning script
wrote on Tuesday. On Wednesday a colleague noticed that the script
counted every patient whose outcome was never ascertained as
event-free, and fixed it. You re-ran the cleaning script and the
model. You did not re-run the script that writes Table 2, because
nothing told you to. The manuscript now reports risks from
Tuesday's analysis set beside a model fitted to Wednesday's. Every
number is plausible, and no step raised an error. A
dependency-aware pipeline makes that state impossible. It knows
that Table 2 depends on the analysis set, and it rebuilds the
table whenever the analysis set changes.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Make provides a simple mechanism for maintaining up-to-date
versions of programs that result from many operations on a
number of files.*

[Stuart Feldman]{.smallcaps}, *Make: A Program for
Maintaining Computer Programs* (1979)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Where this chapter sits: a pipeline tool organizes the Analyze stage, deciding which derived objects, models, and tables are stale and rebuilding exactly those.](10b-targets_files/figure-pdf/fig-targets-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-targets-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Analyze.' width=100%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'}
**Reading time.** About 20 minutes.

**You'll need.** @sec-rrtools for the compendium layout and the
`R/` directory of functions, and @sec-renv for pinning packages.
Install the package once with `install.packages("targets")`. The
pipeline in this chapter uses:

```r
library(targets)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
```

**You'll be able to.**

- Decompose an analysis into targets, each a function with
  explicit inputs, and declare them in a `_targets.R` file.
- Predict which targets an edit invalidates, and confirm the
  prediction with `tar_outdated()` before running `tar_make()`.
- Declare input files with `format = "file"` so that a new data
  extract invalidates everything downstream of it.
- Make a Quarto report a target, and run the whole pipeline in a
  container.

**Outline.**

## The dependency graph {#sec-targets-dag}

An analysis is a chain of steps: read the raw data, derive the
analysis set, summarize it, fit a model, write the report. When
you change one step, everything downstream of it becomes stale,
and everything upstream remains sound. Doing this bookkeeping by
hand means remembering which steps to re-run after every change.
The errors it produces are silent. That is, a table built from a
stale intermediate looks exactly like a table built from a current
one.

The `targets` package [@landau2021targets] automates the
bookkeeping. You declare the steps. `targets` works out their
dependencies and order, runs only what has changed and what
depends on it, and skips the rest. It is the R successor to GNU
Make, designed around R objects rather than files. The benefit is
partly speed, but mostly trust. When `targets` reports that a
target is up to date, the target reflects the current code and
data. A hand re-run cannot promise that.

The organizing idea is the [**directed acyclic graph**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-dag) (DAG). Each
step is a node; an arrow from step A to step B means B uses A's
output. The graph is 'directed' because dependencies have a
direction. It is 'acyclic' because a step cannot depend on itself,
even indirectly. Given the graph, the order of execution is
determined. So is the set of steps that a change makes stale:
everything reachable by following the arrows forward from the
changed node.
@fig-targets-dag is the graph of the pipeline this chapter builds;
each node is named after its target.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-targets-dag
%%| fig-alt: "Directed acyclic graph of the HF-HOME pipeline. Two
%%|   file targets, rand_file and outcomes_file, feed the targets
%%|   randomization and outcomes. Both feed analysis_set, which
%%|   feeds table_2. A dashed arrow from table_2 to report marks the
%%|   report target added later in the chapter. Editing the
%%|   function behind analysis_set makes analysis_set, table_2, and
%%|   report stale and leaves the four targets above it untouched."
%%| fig-cap: "The dependency graph of the chapter's pipeline, with
%%|   each node named after its target. Editing the function behind
%%|   `analysis_set` makes `analysis_set`, `table_2`, and `report`
%%|   stale and leaves the four targets above it alone; `targets`
%%|   rebuilds exactly the stale nodes. The dashed `report` target
%%|   is added in @sec-targets-report."
flowchart TD
  RF["rand_file"] --> RA["randomization"]
  OF["outcomes_file"] --> OU["outcomes"]
  RA --> AS["analysis_set"]
  OU --> AS
  AS --> T2["table_2"]
  T2 -.-> REP["report"]
```

The graph is only as clear as the decomposition it encodes. You
make the decomposition; the tool only records it. Make each target
a meaningful unit (read, derive, summarize, model, report). Each
should be computed by a function with explicit inputs and one
output, rather than by one thousand-line script that a single
target wraps. A target that does too much is rebuilt for every
small change. A target that does too little clutters the graph
without adding information. We note that the finished plan is also
documentation. `_targets.R` states what depends on what, and it is
often the most useful single file for a collaborator new to the
project.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In @fig-targets-dag, you edit the function behind
`table_2` and run the pipeline. Which targets are rebuilt, and
which are skipped?

**Answer.** `table_2` is rebuilt because its function changed, and
`report` because it depends on `table_2`. The two file targets,
`randomization`, `outcomes`, and `analysis_set` are skipped,
because none of them lies downstream of the change. Everything
upstream, which may be expensive to compute, is left alone.
:::

### Exercises

1. Using @fig-targets-dag, list the targets that become stale when
   (a) a new `outcomes.csv` arrives, and (b) you edit the function
   that reads the randomization file.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) `outcomes_file`, `outcomes`, `analysis_set`, `table_2`, and
`report`: everything reachable forward from `outcomes_file`. The
randomization branch is untouched. (b) `randomization`,
`analysis_set`, `table_2`, and `report`. The function is shared by
both read targets in the pipeline below, so in that pipeline
`outcomes` is stale as well; the graph shows data dependencies,
and `targets` also tracks the functions each target calls.
:::

## A pipeline for the running study {#sec-targets-pipeline}

The pipeline reads the HF-HOME randomization list and outcomes
file, derives the analysis set, and summarizes the primary outcome
by arm as the manuscript's Table 2. The chunks below build it in a
temporary directory, so that running them changes nothing in the
book's own project. In your own work the same files live at the
root of the compendium.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-pipeline")
unlink(proj, recursive = TRUE)
r_dir <- file.path(proj, "R")
dir.create(r_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(proj, "data"))
invisible(file.copy(
  file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")),
  file.path(proj, "data")
))
```
:::


### Functions in `R/`

Each step is a function in the project's `R/` directory. The
reading function keeps `patient_id` as character, because the
identifiers carry leading zeros:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
read_trial_csv <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))
}
```
:::


The first version of the derivation repeats Tuesday's mistake from
the opening on purpose: `coalesce()` turns a missing outcome into
'no event'.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
derive_analysis_set <- function(randomization, outcomes) {
  randomization |>
    inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id",
               relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    mutate(
      arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")),
      event_30d = coalesce(event_30d, 0)
    ) |>
    select(patient_id, arm, event_30d)
}
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summarize_by_arm <- function(analysis_set) {
  analysis_set |>
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      events = sum(event_30d),
      risk_pct = round(100 * mean(event_30d), 1),
      .by = arm
    ) |>
    arrange(arm)
}
```
:::


### The plan

A `targets` project keeps its pipeline definition in a file named
`_targets.R` at the project root. The plan lists the targets; each
`tar_target()` names a step and gives the R expression that
produces it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(targets)
tar_source()
tar_option_set(packages = c("readr", "dplyr"))

list(
  tar_target(rand_file, "data/randomization.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(outcomes_file, "data/outcomes.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(randomization, read_trial_csv(rand_file)),
  tar_target(outcomes, read_trial_csv(outcomes_file)),
  tar_target(analysis_set, derive_analysis_set(randomization, outcomes)),
  tar_target(table_2, summarize_by_arm(analysis_set))
)
```
:::


`tar_source()` sources every script in `R/`. Declaring `rand_file`
and `outcomes_file` with `format = "file"` tells `targets` to watch
the files' contents, so that a new extract invalidates everything
downstream. The dependencies are not declared explicitly. Instead,
`targets` reads them from the code. It notices that `analysis_set`
uses `randomization` and `outcomes`, that `table_2` uses
`analysis_set`, and so on. That is how it builds the graph in
@fig-targets-dag without your drawing it.

`tar_option_set(packages = ...)` names the packages every target
needs. `targets` runs each target in a clean environment. A
`library()` call at the top of a script you sourced interactively
therefore does not carry over. The packages that the functions in
`R/` use must be listed here (or called with `pkg::fn()`). The
functions above call `read_csv()` and `inner_join()` without a
namespace. Without that line, every target after the file targets
would fail.

### Running it

`tar_make()` runs everything that is out of date. Run it from the
project root:[^with-dir]

[^with-dir]: The chunks wrap each call in `withr::with_dir(proj,
    ...)` so that it runs in the temporary project. In a terminal
    you would start R in the project directory and type
    `tar_make()` alone.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
#> + outcomes_file dispatched
#> ✔ outcomes_file completed [63ms, 74.29 kB]
#> + rand_file dispatched
#> ✔ rand_file completed [1ms, 141.25 kB]
#> + outcomes dispatched
#> ✔ outcomes completed [72ms, 15.34 kB]
#> + randomization dispatched
#> ✔ randomization completed [4ms, 17.25 kB]
#> + analysis_set dispatched
#> ✔ analysis_set completed [11ms, 7.42 kB]
#> + table_2 dispatched
#> ✔ table_2 completed [3ms, 234 B]
#> ✔ ended pipeline [351ms, 6 completed, 0 skipped]
```
:::


The first run builds every target, in an order consistent with
the graph. Run it again with nothing changed:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
#> ✔ skipped pipeline [58ms, 6 skipped]
```
:::


Every target is skipped. `tar_read()` retrieves a built target
into the session, and `tar_load()` loads it under its own name:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
table_2_v1 <- withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_read(table_2))
table_2_v1
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   arm             n events risk_pct
#>   <fct>       <int>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Usual care   1216    268     22  
#> 2 Home health  1216    240     19.7
```
:::


Every patient randomized is in the denominator, and the risks are
diluted by the unascertained patients counted as event-free. The
table looks like any other Table 2.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Recompute the summary without `targets`, from the raw files, and
confirm that the stored target matches it. A mismatch would mean
the store holds something the current code does not produce.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rand <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
trial <- merge(rand, outc, by = "patient_id")
events_v1 <- tapply(ifelse(is.na(trial$event_30d), 0,
                           trial$event_30d), trial$arm, sum)
stopifnot(
  nrow(trial) == nrow(rand),
  all(table_2_v1$n == table(trial$arm)[as.character(table_2_v1$arm)]),
  all(table_2_v1$events == events_v1[as.character(table_2_v1$arm)])
)
```
:::


In your own pipeline, `tar_visnetwork()` (which needs the
`visNetwork` package) draws the graph `targets` inferred; compare
it with the one you intended.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model can draft the plan and the functions. What it cannot
supply is the decomposition, so give it yours.

> **Context.** An R analysis in a research compendium. Raw inputs:
> `data/randomization.csv` and `data/outcomes.csv` (one row per
> `patient_id`, a character key with leading zeros). Steps, in
> order: read each file; join them into the analysis set; summarize
> the primary outcome `event_30d` by `arm`; fit
> `glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial)`.
>
> **Constraints.** One `tar_target()` per step listed, no more.
> Each target calls a function in `R/` with its inputs as
> arguments; no function reads a file path or a global variable
> directly. Declare the raw files with `format = "file"`. List the
> packages in `tar_option_set(packages = ...)`. Add no packages
> beyond `targets`, `readr`, and `dplyr`.
>
> **Criteria.** List the edges of the dependency graph you expect
> before writing code. After I run `tar_make()` twice, the second
> run skips every target.

*Failure mode.* Models collapse steps into one target that calls a
script, or have a function read `"data/outcomes.csv"` by path,
which hides the file from `targets` (the Pitfall below). *Check.*
Compare `targets::tar_network(targets_only = TRUE)$edges` with the
edge list the model gave you, and run `tar_make()` twice. The plan
and the column names are structure, not data, and may go to any
approved tool (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You delete the `tar_option_set()` line from
`_targets.R` and run `tar_make()` in a fresh session. Which
targets fail, and why does the same code work when you source the
functions and call them at the console?

**Answer.** The file targets succeed, and the first target that
calls a function from `readr` or `dplyr` fails with 'could not
find function'. Each target runs in a clean environment that sees
only the packages the plan names. At the console, `library(dplyr)`
from earlier in your session is still attached, which is exactly
the ambient state a pipeline is meant to exclude.
:::

### Exercises

2. Without running anything, list every target `table_2` depends
   on, directly or indirectly. Then confirm your list from the
   graph `targets` inferred.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Directly, `analysis_set`; indirectly, `randomization`, `outcomes`,
`rand_file`, and `outcomes_file`. `tar_network()` returns the
inferred graph without drawing it; its `edges` element lists each
arrow as a `from` and `to` pair:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(
  proj, targets::tar_network(targets_only = TRUE)$edges
)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   from          to           
#>   <chr>         <chr>        
#> 1 analysis_set  table_2      
#> 2 outcomes      analysis_set 
#> 3 outcomes_file outcomes     
#> 4 rand_file     randomization
#> 5 randomization analysis_set
```
:::

:::

## Changing a step {#sec-targets-change}

Now make Wednesday's fix: the analysis set should hold the
patients whose outcome was ascertained, with their observed
outcomes, rather than counting the missing ones as event-free.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
derive_analysis_set <- function(randomization, outcomes) {
  randomization |>
    inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id",
               relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    filter(ascertained) |>
    mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health"))) |>
    select(patient_id, arm, event_30d)
}
```
:::


Before running anything, ask `targets` what the edit made stale:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_outdated())
#> [1] "analysis_set" "table_2"
```
:::


`tar_outdated()` lists the targets the next `tar_make()` will
build. Only the derivation and what lies downstream of it are
listed; the file targets and the two reads are current. Run the
pipeline:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
#> + analysis_set dispatched
#> ✔ analysis_set completed [15ms, 7.02 kB]
#> + table_2 dispatched
#> ✔ table_2 completed [21ms, 245 B]
#> ✔ ended pipeline [241ms, 2 completed, 4 skipped]
table_2_v2 <- withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_read(table_2))
table_2_v2
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   arm             n events risk_pct
#>   <fct>       <int>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Usual care   1133    268     23.7
#> 2 Home health  1136    240     21.1
```
:::


The two reads are skipped and the two stale targets are rebuilt.
The fix to the derivation reached Table 2 without your having to
remember it, so the failure in the opening cannot recur. Consider
a pipeline whose model fit takes an hour. There the same mechanism
means that an iteration costs minutes rather than the full hour.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the rebuilt table now counts only ascertained
patients and that the events, which the fix should not change,
are the same.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
obs <- trial[trial$ascertained, ]
stopifnot(
  all(table_2_v2$n == table(obs$arm)[as.character(table_2_v2$arm)]),
  all(table_2_v2$events == table_2_v1$events),
  all(table_2_v2$n < table_2_v1$n)
)
```
:::

:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A file read inside a function is invisible to `targets`.** If a
function opens `"data/outcomes.csv"` by its path, rather than
receiving the path from a `format = "file"` target, `targets`
tracks the function's code but not the file. Suppose you replace
the file with a new extract. Then `tar_outdated()` reports nothing
and `tar_make()` skips everything. Table 2 is stale again, and the
tool reports it as current. The same holds for any global
variable or option a function reads. Pass every input as an argument, and
declare every file with `format = "file"`. Exercise 3 shows the
failure.
:::

Two further assumptions belong to you rather than to the tool.
The first is determinism. That is, a pipeline assumes that the
same inputs produce the same outputs. `targets` gives each target
its own random-number seed, derived from the seed option
(`tar_option_set(seed = ...)`) and the target's name. A simulation
or bootstrap target therefore reproduces its draws however the
pipeline is scheduled. A target that reads the clock or an
unpinned package defeats that. The second assumption is the
environment. The pipeline records code and data, not package
versions; recording versions is the lockfile's job (@sec-renv).

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
When `targets` rebuilds more than you expected, or less, a model
can help you find the hidden dependency.

> **Context.** Below are my `_targets.R`, the functions in `R/`,
> and the output of `tar_outdated()` and of
> `tar_make()` after I changed [describe the one edit].
>
> **Constraints.** Explain using only what is in the code shown.
> Do not suggest `tar_destroy()`, `tar_invalidate()`, or deleting
> `_targets/`.
>
> **Criteria.** For each target that was rebuilt unexpectedly, or
> skipped unexpectedly, name the dependency (a function, a global
> variable, a file read by path, an option) responsible, and the
> line where it appears.

*Failure mode.* The model recommends deleting the store and
rebuilding everything, which makes the symptom disappear and
leaves the hidden dependency in place. *Check.* Make the change
the model proposes, then confirm with `tar_outdated()` that the
same edit now invalidates exactly the targets downstream of it in
@fig-targets-dag (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** After the edit, `tar_outdated()` listed
`analysis_set` and `table_2`. Suppose the edit had only renamed a
local variable inside `derive_analysis_set()`, so that the
function returns exactly the same data. Which targets would
`tar_make()` run?

**Answer.** `analysis_set` would still run, because its function's
code changed. `table_2` would then be skipped: `targets` compares
the new value of `analysis_set` with the stored one, finds them
identical, and treats everything downstream as current. A pipeline
rebuilds what a change could affect and stops where it did not.
:::

### Exercises

3. Copy the project. In the copy, delete the `outcomes_file`
   target and change the `outcomes` target to call
   `read_trial_csv("data/outcomes.csv")`, with the path written
   inside the call, and run `tar_make()`. Then remove the last row
   of `data/outcomes.csv` and ask `tar_outdated()` what is stale.
   Repeat the edit in the original project and compare.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The copy reports nothing stale after the data change; the
original reports the file target and everything downstream of it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
drop_last_row <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  writeLines(lines[-length(lines)], path)
}

hidden <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-hidden")
unlink(hidden, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(hidden)
invisible(file.copy(list.files(proj, full.names = TRUE), hidden,
                    recursive = TRUE))
unlink(file.path(hidden, "_targets"), recursive = TRUE)
plan <- readLines(file.path(hidden, "_targets.R"))
plan <- plan[!grepl("tar_target(outcomes_file", plan, fixed = TRUE)]
plan <- sub("read_trial_csv(outcomes_file)",
            "read_trial_csv(\"data/outcomes.csv\")", plan,
            fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(plan, file.path(hidden, "_targets.R"))
invisible(withr::with_dir(hidden, targets::tar_make(reporter = "silent")))

drop_last_row(file.path(hidden, "data", "outcomes.csv"))
withr::with_dir(hidden, targets::tar_outdated())
#> character(0)

drop_last_row(file.path(proj, "data", "outcomes.csv"))
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_outdated())
#> [1] "analysis_set"  "outcomes_file" "outcomes"      "table_2"
```
:::


The empty result for the copy is the silent failure: the data
changed and the tool vouches that nothing did. In the original,
`outcomes_file` is a file target, so its changed contents
invalidate `outcomes`, `analysis_set`, and `table_2`.
:::

4. From `table_2` after the fix, compute the risk difference in
   percentage points, usual care minus home health, the direction
   the analysis plan uses (@sec-analysis-plan), so that a positive
   value is a reduction.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
risk <- setNames(table_2_v2$risk_pct, table_2_v2$arm)
risk[["Usual care"]] - risk[["Home health"]]
#> [1] 2.6
```
:::


The difference is a few points in favor of home health, computed
from rounded risks. An estimate for the manuscript belongs in its
own target, with a confidence interval. It should be computed from
`analysis_set` rather than from a rounded table. The analysis
plan's primary
estimator is in @sec-analysis-plan.
:::

## The report as a target {#sec-targets-report}

The opening's failure ended in the manuscript, so the pipeline
should end there too. The `report` target sketched in
@fig-targets-dag would call a function of your own that renders
the document. When the report is a Quarto document, use
`tarchetypes::tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")` instead. It
renders the document and reads the `tar_read()` and `tar_load()`
calls inside it. The report then becomes stale whenever a target
it reads changes. The addition to the plan is two lines. They are
display-only here, because they need the `tarchetypes` and
`quarto` packages and a report to render:

```r
library(tarchetypes)

# appended to the list in _targets.R
tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")
```

Inside `report.qmd`, read each result from the store rather than
recomputing it:

````qmd
```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-primary
#| tbl-cap: "Primary outcome by arm"
targets::tar_read(table_2)
```
````

A report that recomputes its numbers in its own chunks, rather
than reading them from targets, is outside the graph again.
`targets` cannot know that the report depends on the analysis set,
and the report can go stale exactly as Table 2 did. @sec-quarto covers the
document itself and the inline numbers it should carry.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague's `report.qmd` builds its own copy of
Table 2 in a chunk, reading the two CSV files and repeating the
derivation, instead of calling `tar_read(table_2)`. You make the
derivation fix in `R/derive.R`. What does `tar_outdated()` list,
and is the rendered report current?

**Answer.** It lists `analysis_set` and `table_2`, not `report`.
`tar_quarto()` found no `tar_read()` or `tar_load()` call in the
document, so the report depends on nothing in the pipeline, and
its copy of the derivation still holds Tuesday's mistake. The
pipeline is current and the report is not. This is the opening's
failure again, one file later. Read every reported number from a
target.
:::

5. Add `tar_quarto()` to a pipeline of your own with a one-table

## Pipelines in the compendium and the container {#sec-targets-compendium}

A `targets` pipeline fits naturally inside the research
compendium of @sec-rrtools. The `_targets.R` plan and the `R/`
functions live in the package structure, and `renv` (@sec-renv)
pins the packages the pipeline uses. The Dockerfile (@sec-docker)
can end with `CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "targets::tar_make()"]`, so
that running a container from the image executes the entire
analysis. `CMD` runs when the container starts, not when the
image is built. Building only prepares the environment. That is
what you want, since an image that baked in results would have to
be rebuilt for every change to the code.

The store, `_targets/`, holds every built target. Commit
`_targets.R` and the `R/` functions; keep `_targets/` out of Git,
because it is a build product that `tar_make()` regenerates. In a
container, mount the project directory so that the store outlives
the container, or every run starts from nothing.

| Piece | Holds | Version-controlled? |
|---|---|---|
| `_targets.R` | The plan: targets and their commands | Yes |
| `R/` | The functions the targets call | Yes |
| `data/raw_data/` | Inputs declared with `format = "file"` | As @sec-rrtools describes |
| `_targets/` | The store of built targets and their metadata | No |
| `renv.lock` | Package versions the pipeline runs under | Yes |

: Where a pipeline's pieces live in a compendium. {#tbl-targets-pieces}

The compendium holds the code, data, and environment; `targets`
runs the steps in dependency order and reruns only what has
changed. With both in place, the analysis can be re-run end to
end, which the compendium alone does not guarantee.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague builds the image, runs the container
without mounting the project, and reports that every run takes the
full hour. Why?

**Answer.** Without a mount, `_targets/` is written inside the
container's writable layer and discarded when the container
exits. Each run starts with an empty store, so every target is
out of date. Mount the project directory (`-v "$PWD":/work`, as in
@sec-docker) and the store persists between runs.
:::

### Exercises

6. Add a `CMD` line that runs `targets::tar_make()` to the

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The first run's output ends with every target completed; the

so that `_targets/` is written to the host.
:::

## Run logging and audit trails {#sec-targets-logging}

`tar_outdated()` and `tar_make()` answer 'what is stale' and 'build
it'. Neither answers a different question a collaborator, a
reviewer, or a regulator may ask later: what exactly ran, when, on
which R and package versions, and did it finish without warnings.
`targets` keeps part of that answer already, in the metadata
alongside the store.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_meta(fields = c(
  seconds, warnings, error
)))
#> # A tibble: 9 x 4
#>   name                seconds warnings error
#>   <chr>                 <dbl> <chr>    <chr>
#> 1 outcomes_file         0.063 <NA>     <NA> 
#> 2 rand_file             0.001 <NA>     <NA> 
#> 3 outcomes              0.072 <NA>     <NA> 
#> 4 randomization         0.004 <NA>     <NA> 
#> 5 summarize_by_arm     NA     <NA>     <NA> 
#> 6 derive_analysis_set  NA     <NA>     <NA> 
#> 7 read_trial_csv       NA     <NA>     <NA> 
#> 8 analysis_set          0.015 <NA>     <NA> 
#> 9 table_2               0.021 <NA>     <NA>
```
:::


`tar_meta()` returns one row per target with its build time, any
warning or error it raised, and (with other fields) the hash of
its code and data, which is what `tar_outdated()` reads to decide
staleness. It is the pipeline's own bookkeeping. It was not
written to be read on its own as an account of a run in an audit
file. That becomes a gap once a pipeline's output feeds a
regulatory submission.

Two of the gaps in `tar_meta()` as an audit record should be named
before we reach for another tool. First, it describes the store,
not a single execution. A target with `seconds = 0.3` and no error
could have been built just now, or weeks ago on a different
machine, and `tar_meta()` alone does not say which. (`tar_meta()`
does include a `time` field recording the most recent build's
timestamp. However, a submission-grade run log usually wants the
start and end of a whole pipeline execution, not of each target
separately.) Second, it records nothing about the R session that
built the targets beyond what the project's `renv.lock` separately
pins. Suppose a target was built under an R or package version
that later drifted from the lockfile. `tar_meta()` would not flag
it, but `renv::status()` would (@sec-renv). A run log meant to
satisfy an external reviewer needs both records. That is, it needs
a session-level record of what ran and when, and a target-level
record of what each target depended on.

### Structured logging in general-purpose R

Two packages add structured logging to ordinary R code, independent
of `targets`. `logger` writes leveled log entries (`INFO`, `WARN`,
`ERROR`) to a file or the console, with a layout you control, in the
spirit of logging frameworks from other languages. `cli` is aimed
more at readable, formatted console output for a package's users
than at a durable audit record, but its structured message types are
sometimes pressed into the same role. Neither is installed in this
book's environment, so the pattern below is display-only:

```r
library(logger)
log_threshold(INFO)
log_info('starting analysis_set derivation, {nrow(randomization)} rows')
```

These give a pipeline step a log line it would not otherwise have.
However, you have to write good `logger` calls by hand, at every
step that matters, and nothing checks that you did it
consistently.

### Run-logging tools built for an audit trail

Two R packages, both on CRAN as of this writing, are built
specifically to produce a record of a script's execution. The
record is meant to serve as an audit trail, in the sense regulated
clinical trial programming gives that phrase. The packages are the
`pharmaverse` ecosystem's `logrx` [@pharmaverse2025logrx], and
Novo Nordisk's `whirl` [@novonordisk2025whirl]. Both target
clinical programming workflows more directly than general data
science. They are therefore worth knowing about, but not worth
reaching for by default.

`logrx` wraps the execution of a single R script and writes a log.
The log records the code that ran and the session information (R
version, attached packages and their versions, platform). It also
flags any function call from a package that is not on an approved
list. That detail makes it useful for a submission where every
function used must be traceable to a validated package. `whirl`
runs one or more scripts (`whirl::run()`, with an option to run
them in parallel). Using the Quarto command line tool, it writes
each script its own human-readable HTML log. The log records the
script's status (ran clean, warned, or errored), the executed
code, the timestamp, and the session's package versions. `whirl`
also writes a summary page across all the scripts in a batch.

Neither package knows about `targets`' dependency graph. What each
adds is a readable, archivable artifact of one execution, which
`tar_meta()` does not produce. A pipeline that must satisfy an
audit requirement can run `tar_make()` from inside a script that
`whirl` or `logrx` wraps. The resulting log then records the whole
pipeline run (R version, package versions, start and end time).
It sits alongside the metadata `targets` itself keeps about which
targets built and which were current. Treat this as a pointer, not
as a recommendation to adopt either package. Check its current
documentation against your submission's requirements first. Both
are actively maintained, and neither is installed here, so every
code block above is display-only.

Which of `logrx` and `whirl` fits a given project depends on how the
scripts are organized. `logrx` wraps one script at a time and leans
toward flagging unapproved function calls, which suits a submission
whose validation plan names an approved package list. `whirl` runs
one or several scripts, in parallel if asked, and produces a
Quarto-rendered log per script plus a batch summary, which suits a
pipeline broken into several standalone programs rather than one
`targets` plan. Either sits beside `targets` rather than inside
it. The log records that the pipeline ran and under what
environment. `tar_meta()` and `tar_outdated()` remain the tools
that say whether what ran was actually current.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A collaborator asks, 'does `tar_meta()` give us
enough of an audit trail for a submission?' What is missing, and
what would `whirl` or `logrx` add that it does not?

**Answer.** `tar_meta()` tells you which targets are current and how
long each took to build; it is a cache's own bookkeeping, not a
report meant to be read by someone outside the project. It does not
record the R version, the attached package versions, or the exact
code that executed, in one human-readable document. `whirl` or
`logrx` wrap the run and produce exactly that: a log, readable
without re-running anything, of what ran, under what environment,
with what result. A submission needs both records.
:::

7. A reviewer asks for proof that the version of R and the package

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
First, `renv::status()` inside the environment that ran the
pipeline: a mismatch shows as a report that the lockfile names
different package versions than are installed, or a different R
version than `sessionInfo()` reports. Second, a run-logging tool
(`whirl::run()` or `logrx`) wrapping the script that calls
`tar_make()`: its log records the session information actually in
effect during that run, which can be compared line by line against
`renv.lock`. `tar_meta()` alone answers neither question, because it
records target-level build metadata, not session-level package
versions.
:::

## Make and Snakemake beside targets {#sec-targets-make}

`targets` is not the only dependency-aware build tool. A
biostatistician moves between ecosystems often enough that the
other two are worth comparing with it.

**GNU Make**, the tool the chapter's epigraph credits, is older,
far more widely installed, and language-agnostic. It ships on
nearly every Unix-like system. A `Makefile` can orchestrate steps
written in R, Python, shell, or anything else, by calling each as
a command-line program. Its staleness check is the file's
modification timestamp, not the content or the code that produced
it. That is both Make's simplicity and its limitation. Touching a
file without changing its content makes Make think it is stale.
Conversely, editing the function behind a target without touching
any file on disk makes Make think nothing changed. That is the
everyday case `targets` tracks correctly through `tar_outdated()`.
Make is a reasonable choice for joining steps in different
languages at a coarse grain (run the R pipeline, then a Python
script, then a report). It is a poor substitute for `targets`'
fine-grained, R-object-aware caching inside an R analysis.

**Snakemake** is the Python ecosystem's closer analogue to
`targets`. It is a workflow manager built around rules with
declared inputs and outputs, assembled into a dependency graph,
with its own staleness checking. It also has strong support for
scaling a pipeline across a cluster's job scheduler, including
SLURM (@sec-cloud-hpc). It needs far less hand-written
batch-script boilerplate than @sec-cloud shows for a bare job
array. Snakemake is close to a common language in bioinformatics
and computational-biology groups. A biostatistician who
collaborates with such a group will meet it on the Python side of
a mixed project, even when the statistical analysis stays in R.

### Python interoperability from an R-primary compendium

A project that is R-primary but needs one Python step (an
off-the-shelf machine learning library, say, with no R equivalent)
has two ways to call it without leaving the `targets` pipeline.
`reticulate` embeds a Python session inside the R session. A
`tar_target()` can then call a Python function and receive its
result back directly as an R object. The cost is that both
languages' environments (an R library and a Python environment)
must be kept pinned and compatible. That doubles the surface
@sec-renv and @sec-docker have to cover. The plainer alternative
is to shell out. That is, a target's command is
`system2('python3', c('script.py', input_path))`. The Python
script reads and writes files that are themselves `targets` inputs
and outputs (`format = "file"` on each side of the boundary).
Shelling out loses `reticulate`'s convenient object passing.
However, it keeps the two languages' package management fully
separate. It is often the simpler choice for a single well-defined
step, as opposed to a continuously interleaved R-and-Python
analysis.

R and Python can be mixed under any of these tools; the choice is
which ecosystem's tool organizes the whole pipeline. Both Make and
Snakemake can call out to R exactly as easily as a `targets`
pipeline can call out to Python.

The practical rule of thumb for a mostly-R biostatistics project is
to let the language that does most of the analytical work own the
pipeline, and to treat the other language's steps as single,
well-defined targets or rules rather than interleaving the two
throughout. Consider a project whose pipeline calls `reticulate`
from inside one `tar_target()` and also shells out to `Rscript`
from inside one Snakemake `rule`. That usually means the team
never settled the question. It is paying the cost of both tools'
setup at once: two lockfiles (`renv.lock` and a Python environment
file), two dependency graphs to reason about, and two places a
stale intermediate could hide. Settling it early, even informally, is
worth more than either tool's specific features.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A collaborator proposes rewriting this chapter's
`targets` pipeline in Make, arguing that 'everyone already has
`make`'. What would the team lose?

**Answer.** Make's staleness check is the file timestamp. The
pipeline would therefore have to read and write every intermediate
(the analysis set, the table) to a file. A change to a function's
code with no file touched would go undetected, unless the Makefile
recipe also hashed the function source. `targets` already does
that work.
The team would gain ubiquity and language-agnosticism and lose
`targets`' R-object-aware dependency tracking, `tar_outdated()`'s
prediction of what will rebuild, and the ability to keep
intermediate results as R objects rather than serialized files at
every step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

The consideration is which language the team is more fluent in for
maintaining the pipeline's own logic (not just the analysis code).
A team that works in Python day to day will find Snakemake's rules

step, may prefer to keep `targets` as the organizing tool. It
would treat Python as a dependency called from one target, the way
this section's `reticulate` and shell-out options do.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: derived data are a build product.** Let the pipeline
   regenerate every intermediate; never edit or hand-run one into
   place.
2. **Habit 8: a stale intermediate produces a plausible number.**
   Run `tar_outdated()` before you report anything, and pass every
   input as an argument so that it can see the change.
3. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The pipeline tracks code and
   data; the lockfile and the container pin what it runs on.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code |
|---|---|
| Source the functions in `R/` | `tar_source()` |
| Declare packages for every target | `tar_option_set(packages = c(...))` |
| Declare a target | `tar_target(name, command)` |
| Watch an input file's contents | `tar_target(f, "data/x.csv", format = "file")` |
| Run what is out of date | `tar_make()` |
| List what the next run will build | `tar_outdated()` |
| Retrieve a target | `tar_read(name)`, or `tar_load(name)` |
| Inspect the inferred graph | `tar_network()`, or `tar_visnetwork()` with `visNetwork` |
| Make a Quarto report a target | `tarchetypes::tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")` |
| Run the pipeline in a container | `CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "targets::tar_make()"]` |

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10b}

1. A dependency-aware tool rebuilds exactly the steps that
   are downstream of the change and leaves the rest alone,
   and it guarantees that nothing stale survives. Re-sourcing
   all your scripts by hand either wastes time re-running
   unchanged steps or, worse, forgets a step and leaves a
   downstream result built from a stale intermediate.
2. A directed acyclic graph is a set of nodes connected by
   arrows that have a direction and form no cycles. It is
   the right abstraction because an analysis step depends on
   its inputs (direction) and cannot depend on itself
   (acyclic), so the graph determines both the execution
   order and the set of steps a change makes stale.
3. The symptom means you cannot attribute a change in
   results to a specific step, which is exactly the
   bookkeeping a pipeline tool maintains. `targets` records
   what each target depended on, so a change to a tracked
   input is traceable to the step it affects and marks that
   step stale. The guarantee covers only what `targets` can
   see: a file read inside a function (the Pitfall in
   @sec-targets-change) escapes it.
